title: Machine Learning Introduction
subtitle: A practical introduction to learning from data
sections: What does a model learn?

Machine learning is a way to build software that discovers useful patterns in examples. A model receives data, applies a mathematical rule, and returns a prediction. Training adjusts that rule so predictions fit the examples more closely. The goal is not simply to remember the training data. A useful model should generalize to new observations collected under similar conditions.

Imagine predicting the demand for a neighborhood bicycle service. Historical rentals, temperature, day of the week, and rainfall can become features. The number of rentals is the target. Before training a model, we inspect missing values, unusual measurements, and changes in how the data was collected. Clean data and a clear question often matter more than a complicated algorithm.
Learning with examples

Supervised learning uses examples with known targets. Regression predicts a quantity such as demand, while classification predicts a category such as whether an order needs review. Unsupervised learning explores data without predefined targets. Clustering, for example, can group observations that share similar characteristics. These groups are useful descriptions, but they do not automatically explain why a pattern exists.

A baseline is a simple prediction rule that gives us a starting point. For bicycle rentals, yesterday's demand or an average for the same weekday might be a useful baseline. A complex model should improve on that baseline in a meaningful way. We compare models with a metric that reflects the actual decision, rather than choosing whichever score looks most impressive.
Evaluating responsibly

We separate training data from evaluation data before fitting transformations or selecting features. Information from the evaluation set must not leak into training. When observations follow a timeline, a chronological split may be more realistic than a random split. Cross-validation can estimate how much results vary across different subsets, but its design must respect the structure of the data.

Accuracy is only one part of evaluation. We also look at error patterns, performance for relevant groups, stability, and the cost of a wrong prediction. A model that performs well on average may still fail in important situations. Documenting assumptions helps the next developer understand what was tested and what remains uncertain.
From experiment to useful system

A reliable learning system includes more than its model. Data validation, versioned experiments, clear outputs, and monitoring make results easier to maintain. We record the dataset, the training configuration, the evaluation method, and the limitations. When data changes, previous performance estimates may stop being representative.

For a first project, start with a small dataset and an understandable baseline. Build the simplest complete workflow: inspect data, split it, train, evaluate, and explain the result. The strongest project tells a clear story about a real question and shows how evidence supports its conclusions.

title: Python Programming Guide
subtitle: Small building blocks for readable, dependable programs
sections: Values and useful structures

Python programs work with values such as strings, numbers, and booleans. Variables give those values names so that a program can describe an idea clearly. Prefer names that explain a purpose: document_count communicates more than a single letter. Readable code reduces the effort needed to understand what happens and why it happens.

Lists preserve an ordered collection of values. Dictionaries associate keys with values and are useful for structured information such as a document's title and page count. Sets represent unique items and make membership checks convenient. Choosing the right structure often simplifies a program more than adding clever control flow.
Functions and responsibilities

A function collects a useful operation behind a clear name. A good function usually has one responsibility, receives the values it needs, and returns a result that callers can use. Separating calculation from file access makes both operations easier to test. A text analysis function, for example, can accept a string without knowing where that string came from.

Default arguments and keyword arguments make interfaces easier to read, but mutable default values need care. Use None when a new list or dictionary should be created for each call. Type hints document expected inputs and outputs; they improve editor feedback and help explain an interface, while runtime validation still checks untrusted values.
Files, errors and resources

Use a context manager when working with a file so the resource closes reliably. Explicit text encodings prevent surprises when a project moves between machines. Paths should be assembled with a path library rather than by joining arbitrary strings. User-provided filenames should never be trusted as storage paths.

Errors are part of normal software behavior. Catch the errors an operation can reasonably recover from, explain the problem clearly, and preserve useful diagnostic information for developers. Avoid hiding every exception behind a successful result. If writing a file and a database record forms one operation, plan what happens when either step fails.
Testing and project habits

A useful test checks observable behavior with representative inputs. Include empty input, unusual characters, invalid values, and access boundaries where they matter. Tests should make failures easy to understand and should run without relying on a live external service. Temporary directories and isolated databases keep tests predictable.

Create a virtual environment for each project and record its dependencies. Keep secrets outside source control and document the commands needed to run the application. Consistent formatting, short modules, and meaningful names make a project easier to extend. The best Python code leaves the next reader with fewer questions.

title: Natural Language Processing Notes
subtitle: Turning text into patterns you can inspect
sections: Text is structured information

Natural language processing explores how software can work with human language. Text contains meaning, but it also contains observable patterns: words, punctuation, repeated phrases, and relationships between sentences. A practical analysis starts by deciding which patterns will help answer a question. A document dashboard can reveal frequent terms without claiming to understand every idea in the document.

The first step is often tokenization, which divides text into units. Word tokens can be useful for frequency statistics, while sentence tokens support readability estimates. Different tokenization rules handle punctuation, contractions, and compound terms differently. Write down the rule so that users understand what a count represents.
Normalization and stopwords

Normalization makes comparisons more consistent. Case folding treats Learning and learning as the same word for many frequency tasks. Whitespace cleanup helps readability, while preserving paragraph boundaries retains some document structure. Removing punctuation may help one analysis but discard useful information for another. The appropriate choices depend on the question.

Stopwords are frequent function words such as the, and, or of. Filtering them can make a keyword list easier to scan. A stopword list is a useful heuristic rather than a universal definition of meaningful language. Domain-specific terms may also need filtering. Always keep the original extracted text available so that users can inspect the evidence.
Frequency and lexical diversity

A frequency table counts how often each token occurs. Sorting that table reveals repeated terms and supports a simple bar chart. Frequency can point to a topic, but repetition does not prove importance. Boilerplate, repeated headers, and extraction artifacts may appear often too. Reviewing the document alongside the chart keeps the analysis grounded.

Lexical diversity compares the number of unique words with the total word count. A short document can have a higher ratio than a long document even when both use varied language. Use the ratio as a descriptive statistic and avoid treating it as a quality score. Similarly, reading time is an estimate based on an assumed reading speed.
Going beyond counts

Search connects a statistical overview to specific passages. Literal case-insensitive search is predictable and easy to explain. Snippets show the context surrounding each match, while highlighted page text helps users locate the full passage. Search results must remain safely escaped when displayed in a web interface.

More advanced analysis can include named entities, topics, summaries, and language-specific tokenization. Each approach introduces assumptions and evaluation requirements. Begin with transparent statistics, retain context, and clearly describe limitations. A trustworthy text tool helps users inspect its results instead of asking them to accept unexplained conclusions.

title: Data Mining Overview
subtitle: Finding useful patterns without losing their context
sections: Begin with a question

Data mining searches a collection of observations for useful relationships and patterns. A clear question guides the process: which transactions are unusual, which events happen together, or which customers have similar needs? Without a question, it is easy to find interesting-looking results that have no practical value. Define the decision the analysis will support before choosing a technique.

A dataset carries the history of how it was collected. Missing observations, changing definitions, and measurement errors can affect every result. Inspect distributions and examples, ask what each column means, and record the data source. A pattern in a sample may not represent the wider population.
Preparation and exploration

Preparation includes checking types, handling missing values, removing genuine duplicates, and creating useful features. A duplicate is not always an error: two identical transactions may represent separate events. Transformations should preserve enough information to explain their effects. Keep a record of important choices so the workflow can be repeated.

Exploratory charts make distributions and relationships visible. Compare groups carefully and look for changes over time. Summary statistics help describe a dataset, but a single average can hide several distinct groups. Combining numerical summaries with representative examples creates a more accurate picture.
Patterns and interpretation

Clustering groups observations by similarity. Association rules describe items that appear together, such as products in a shopping basket. Anomaly detection identifies observations that differ from a reference pattern. Each method depends on a definition of similarity, frequency, or unusual behavior, and those definitions should match the problem.

A discovered relationship is not automatically causal. A third factor may explain why two measurements move together. Testing many possible patterns also increases the chance of finding something by accident. Use held-out data, domain knowledge, and careful validation to distinguish reliable findings from coincidences.
Communicating useful results

A useful report explains what was measured, what was found, and how much confidence the evidence supports. Include the sample size, the time period, and relevant limitations. Visualizations should label their axes and use scales that make comparisons fair. Avoid presenting a model score without explaining the decision it informs.

Responsible analysis considers privacy and the effects of acting on a result. Collect only the information needed for the question, control access, and review potential harms. A strong data mining project connects a reproducible workflow with a modest, evidence-based conclusion that another person can inspect.

title: Web Development Fundamentals
subtitle: From a browser request to a reliable user experience
sections: The request and response cycle

A browser requests a resource from a server and receives a response. The response may contain an HTML page, a stylesheet, a script, or structured data. URLs identify resources, while HTTP methods describe the kind of operation being requested. Reading a page and deleting a record are different actions and should use appropriate methods.

A web application connects interface design with server behavior. HTML gives content structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript adds interaction. The server validates requests, enforces access rules, and reads or writes persistent data. A pleasant interface depends on all of these pieces working together.
Accessible interfaces

Semantic elements make a page easier to navigate and understand. Forms need visible labels, helpful validation messages, and keyboard-accessible controls. Buttons should describe actions, while links should lead to resources. A visible focus indicator helps people understand where keyboard interaction will happen.

Responsive layouts adapt to available space. A dashboard can use a multi-column grid on a desktop and stacked cards on a phone. Tables may need their own scroll container rather than causing the entire page to overflow. Test long filenames, empty states, loading states, and narrow viewports as part of interface design.
Authentication and data access

Authentication identifies an account, while authorization decides what that account can do. A signed-in user should not gain access to another user's documents by changing an identifier in a URL. Ownership checks belong on the server for every read, export, and deletion operation. Hiding a button is helpful presentation, but it does not enforce access.

Passwords should be stored as hashes rather than readable strings. CSRF protection helps prevent a different site from submitting actions through a user's session. Environment variables keep configuration and secrets separate from source code. Uploaded files remain untrusted even when their extension looks correct.
Building a maintainable project

Separate application features into modules with clear responsibilities. Routes coordinate a request; services implement operations; models describe persistent data. Templates render an interface without performing complex business logic. This structure makes a project easier to test and lets a developer change one layer without rewriting everything.

Document the installation steps and verify them in a fresh environment. Database migrations preserve schema history, while demo data helps reviewers explore the application quickly. Automated tests should cover successful workflows and important failure boundaries. A portfolio project feels complete when its design, behavior, documentation, and tests tell the same story.
